analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting and even-age logging on federal forest lands and lets citizens sue to enforce it.
analysis.headline: The clearcutting ban drew 69 cosponsors but died in four House committees; its only action after introduction was a single subcommittee hearing in June 1992.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited clearcutting and other even-age logging on every forest the federal government manages for timber — national forests, Bureau of Land Management land, wildlife refuges, Indian forest lands, and military reservations. Within a year, each site would have had to switch to selection logging (cutting scattered individual trees and small groups while the forest keeps a continuous canopy) or stop timber management and restore native biodiversity. It also let any citizen sue to enforce the ban, with courts able to impose penalties of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation and award attorney's fees, and it stripped the government of its usual immunity from such suits.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use or depend on federal forests: the bill's stated aim was conserving native biodiversity, preventing soil erosion, protecting water quality and fisheries from stream sedimentation, and preserving deep-canopy forest for recreation. Its findings also argued selection logging is more labor-intensive than clearcutting, meaning more jobs per board foot of timber, and produces higher-quality sawlogs.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits all even-age logging and even-age management — clearcutting, salvage, seed-tree, and shelterwood cutting — on national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, Indian forest lands, and military lands, one year after enactment.
Directs agencies to shift each existing site to selection management within a year, or stop managing it for timber and let native biodiversity return.

Creates a citizen enforcement right: any person can sue, including against the United States, for injunctions and civil penalties of $5,000–$50,000 per violation, with attorney's fees awarded and sovereign immunity waived, with no notice required.
The bill's findings state that selection logging is more job-intensive than even-age cutting for the same timber output and yields higher-quality sawlogs.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which buys federal timber and relies on cheap, efficient even-age harvests; sawmills and rural logging communities dependent on federal timber supply; and the Treasury, which under the bill would pay judgments and penalties out of the Judgment Fund when the government itself was found in violation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies and dependent mill towns

drawbacks.text: The ban applies across the board with a one-year deadline and no regional exceptions, including wildlife refuges and Indian forest lands, which would force abrupt changes in forest management and timber sale programs regardless of local conditions.

Even-age harvesting is the least expensive way to harvest timber; restricting it on federal lands would reduce timber sale volume and raise logging costs, with job and revenue effects concentrated in timber-dependent rural communities.
The bill waives sovereign immunity and lets any citizen sue without prior notice, with mandatory attorney's fees, which agencies and timber purchasers would bear as litigation risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The conservation and water-quality gains would be broad and public, and the bill itself claimed more jobs from selection logging; but the one-year, no-exceptions mandate was blunt, and the adjustment costs would fall hardest on mill towns and workers in regions where federal timber feeds local mills. A more gradual or regionally tailored phase-out would have addressed the strongest objection.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in four House committees for the entire two-year Congress; after a subcommittee referral and one hearing, no committee ever voted to report it and the House never voted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Bryant of Texas introduced the bill on April 22, 1991, and it was referred to four committees: Agriculture, Interior and Insular Affairs, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Armed Services.
It was sent to subcommittees, and executive comments were requested from the Departments of Agriculture, Interior, and Defense.

The only substantive action after that was a subcommittee hearing on June 16, 1992; no committee ever reported the bill and no vote was ever taken in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber buyers and the logging industry kept clearcutting federal forests uninterrupted, and the agencies' existing management practices were never legally challenged under the new standards. Forest users got none of the biodiversity, water-quality, or citizen-enforcement protections.

for.name: Rep. John W. Bryant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Forest Biodiversity and Clearcutting Prohibition Act of 1991 on April 22, 1991.

for.name: 69 House cosponsors
for.role: Members signing onto the bill (56 Democrats, 13 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Scheuer, Kostmayer, Bonior, Mineta, and Boehlert among others.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the rest of the Congress; referred it to a subcommittee and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Rep. E. (Kika) de la Garza
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: of the 69 cosponsors, 56 were Democrats and 13 were Republicans, and the bill's opposition came from committee inaction rather than a recorded vote.

industries.note: The industry buys federal timber and relies on clearcutting as its cheapest, most efficient harvest method; the bill would have ended even-age harvesting on all federal forest land. The public owns these forests, so the industry's gain from blocking the bill ran against the resource's owners.
Mills dependent on federal timber sales would face reduced supply and higher logging costs under selection management; rural mill towns would bear much of the adjustment.
The bill's findings tie even-age logging to stream sedimentation and siltation that impair fish spawning; ending it was framed as protecting fishing resources.
